title: The UK productivity crisis was a statistical error: 0.7% became 1.3%
dek: Fifteen years of Britain being cast as the worst performer on productivity among developed economies may just be the ONS miscounting hours worked — counting people on holiday as working 40 hours, inflating the denominator and pushing productivity down.
why: Medium information density, but the UK productivity revision alone is enough to change your read on the "British disease"; the other three segments are routine fact-checks you can take or leave.
who: Investors and researchers following the UK economy, the macro productivity narrative, or who need to cite UK official statistics; anyone investing in data centres and grid infrastructure should see the third segment.
skip: The Irish clergy segment (7:26-13:38) is a pure fact-check, unrelated to the rest, and can be skipped.

points.h: The UK productivity crisis was calculated into existence
points.body: After the financial crisis, UK productivity growth was estimated at 0.7% a year, the worst in the developed world, and it became the raw material for fifteen years of the "productivity puzzle." After the ONS changed how it measures hours worked, that figure became 1.3%, nearly double. Output and GDP did not change; only the denominator did: Britons actually work far fewer hours than previously thought. Chris Giles says pre-crisis growth was 2%, and 2% means productivity doubles roughly every 35 years, while 0.7% means it takes a century to double; 1.3% falls in between. Britain is no longer an international outlier, but growth is still below the pre-crisis rate.

points.h: Asking people how many hours they work cannot be trusted
points.body: The old method simply asked respondents how many hours they worked in a week and took the answer at face value. The problem was follow-up visits: if no one answered the door in August, the ONS carried over the 40 hours that person had reported three months earlier, plugging in a 40 — when that person was probably on holiday and had not worked a single hour. The OECD recommended back in 2018 that countries stop doing this; the UK took eight years to change. Giles says that during those eight years people wrote a batch of "UK productivity crisis" articles that no longer hold up. He admits this is maddening, but the change is in the right direction.

points.h: One in ten Irish people becoming clergy is a myth
points.body: The book said that in the 1960s one in every ten Irish children became a nun, priest or Christian Brother. The 1961 census showed 18,854 Catholic clergy and nuns, 2,125 Christian Brothers and other religious brothers, and 4,842 seminarians — 25,821 in total, or 1/104 of the population. The 1951 ratio was 1/127. The original source is research by Mary Daly, who looked only at students sitting the leaving certificate exam in 1966, when fewer than 20% of the school-age population took that exam — about 12,000 people, roughly one in ten of whom entered religious life. That qualifier was lost in retelling and became "all children." The author has said subsequent editions will be corrected.

points.h: Grid queue numbers are inflated by applications
points.body: Between November 2024 and June 2025, cumulative electricity demand in the UK grid connection queue jumped from about 41 GW to 125 GW, tripling in six months, with data centres accounting for 73 GW. But queuing is cheap, like booking a table at a popular restaurant months in advance; many projects will never actually be built or will shrink. Ofgem estimates that if all this data centre demand materialised, the cost would be close to £700 billion, nearly a quarter of UK annual GDP. A 2025 government report projected 6 GW would be needed by 2030, while another queue analysis reckoned about 20 GW has serious financial backing behind it. Johnny Gowdy of Regen says nobody knows how much will ultimately get built.

points.h: The data centre emissions comparison counts only direct emissions
points.body: Foxglove's analysis said two planned data centres at full load would emit more carbon than ExxonMobil's UK operations. That comparison counts only ExxonMobil's own operational emissions, excluding the petrol and diesel it sells — which is the main source of emissions, something ordinary readers may not spot. Foxglove also assumed the data centres run at 100% power year-round, while a scholar studying AI's carbon footprint used 65%. More important is the power source: the planning documents for these two projects say that initially, because they cannot connect to the grid, they will use on-site gas generation. The UK grid as a whole gets about half its power from renewables and only 30% from gas, so these data centres amount to stimulating demand for higher-carbon generation.

points.h: Vinyl's physical constraint actually got weaker
points.body: The 1950s claim was this: the closer a record gets to the centre, the lower the linear speed, and the less bass and brightness a groove can hold, so you put the quiet song at the end of a side. Mitchell Sterling's database has 2,284 albums and 27,000 songs, spanning 1953 to the present. Measured by relative loudness, before 1982 closing tracks averaged about 0.65 dB quieter than earlier tracks; after 1982, when cassette sales overtook vinyl in the US and the constraint disappeared, the gap actually widened to about 1.5 dB. In the streaming era after 2010, the gap is still twice what it was in the vinyl era. In other words, the less the physical constraint mattered, the quieter closing tracks became.

points.h: The quiet ending went from constraint to artistic device
points.body: Sterling defines a quiet, acoustic closing track as the "typical quiet acoustic farewell." In the 1950s, more than 60% of albums ended with a quiet, acoustic song; as recordings overall got louder, that absolute share slid all the way down to under one-sixth in the 1980s; by the 2000s and 2020s it had climbed back to about one-third. Sterling's analogy is the save icon on a floppy disk: the constraint is long gone, the habit remains. He also found in streaming data that an album's last track averages longer, more acoustic and sadder — but that is an average, and hip-hop, heavy metal and electronic music are full of loud exceptions.
